description:
OrbitFlare is an Earth-observation and data science team exploring how satellite data can help us better understand our planet.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are working on harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS active fire observations to create a more consistent historical record of thermal activity.

Our goal is to combine satellite data processing, statistical analysis and interactive visualization into an accessible fire-intelligence platform.

We welcome interested collaborators
summary: OrbitFlare is a web app that joins NASA’s two satellite fire records, MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward), into one consistent burning activity calendar. The sensors count fires on different scales: VIIRS sees about 6.1 times more hotspots than MODIS in the same place and months, so joining them as they are creates a fake jump in 2012. We harmonised them with monthly scale factors fitted on the 167 months when both sensors ran, then chained S-NPP to NOAA-20 because S-NPP data ends in November 2026. In a leave-one-year-out test the method predicts real VIIRS counts with 0.97 monthly correlation and about 8% error in yearly totals. Users draw an area on a map or type coordinates, pick dates, and get a year-by-month calendar, a comparison with the usual for each month, a monthly chart and CSV downloads. For the Pune to Nashik region it shows burning peaking in March and an unusually active October 2026. The tool helps emergency managers, scientists and land managers spot unusual fire periods early.
details:
What it does: Harmonises NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one 2003–2026 record and shows it as a burning activity calendar for any area drawn on the map.

How it works: (1) Keep VIIRS detections rated nominal or high and MODIS at 30% confidence or more. (2) Before Feb 2012, scale each MODIS hotspot by a calendar-month factor (4.8× in January to 13.1× in June), fitted on 167 overlapping months. (3) Use VIIRS S-NPP to Mar 2018, then NOAA-20 divided by 1.007. NOAA-21 is a cross-check. Leave-one-year-out test: 0.97 monthly correlation, 8% yearly error, 18% error for Nov–May months.

Benefits and impact: Emergency managers, scientists and land managers can see which months and years burned most, compare the current month with the historical median, and download CSVs.

Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy) for analysis. The app is one HTML page in plain JavaScript with no outside libraries, so it works offline.

Creative choices: Colour-blind-safe blue/orange “versus usual” view. A choice of “usual” (every year or last 10 years). Months with under 10 hotspots are shown grey so small counts don’t look extreme.

Limits: Factors were fitted on the Pune–Nashik area and applied to sub-areas. Hotspots are detections, not burned area. Recent months use near-real-time data that NASA may revise.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System)
FIRMS Archive Download: MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21
